passages.title: Learning materials
passages.quote: Two prose passages were selected from the reading comprehension section of a test-preparation book for the Test of English as a Foreign Language (TOEFL; Rogers, 2001). Each passage covered a single topic (‘‘The Sun’’ and ‘‘Sea Otters’’), and each was divided into 30 idea units for scoring purposes.

passages.title: Outcome measure
passages.quote: Subjects’ recall responses were scored by giving 1 point for each correctly recalled idea unit (out of 30).
passages.verification: Matched to text on the stated PDF page.

passages.title: Comparing schedules
passages.quote: This would be called a 1-5-9 schedule to reflect the number of trials that occurred between each test, and the absolute spacing of the repeated tests would be 15 trials. The appropriate comparison to this expanding condition is a condition matched on absolute spacing but differing in the relative spacing of tests. An equally spaced schedule where the interval between each test is five trials (a 5-5-5 schedule) has the same absolute spacing as the expanding condition but differs in the relative distribution of tests.

passages.title: Retention interval
passages.quote: The learning phase terminated once all repeated tests had occurred. The subjects were then dismissed and returned for the final test 1 week later. The final test included the 24 critical pairs, tested in a random order, and did not include filler items.
passages.verification: Matched to text on the stated PDF page.
passages.context: The final recall test took place one week after learning and included the 24 critical pairs.

passages.title: Spaced versus massed retrieval
passages.quote: However, introducing spacing between the three repeated tests enhanced retention.
passages.verification: Matched to text on the stated PDF page.
passages.context: Spacing the repeated tests improved retention in this experiment relative to massed retrieval. This does not identify a universally optimal daily schedule.
